A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Flow-GRPO. Their main texts, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching retained content across relocation and renumbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original SD3.5-M training and evaluation results, including benchmark scores, generalization tests, and denoising, noise-level and KL analyses.

after.justification: v4 retains original empirical results and adds alignment-method comparisons, qualitative training trajectories and sampling analyses in its appendices.

M1.justification: Section 5.1 revises the specified counting reward from normalized count error to one minus that error, and the OCR reward from character-count discrepancy to clipped normalized edit-distance similarity. These revise task-specific reward objectives; the clipped GRPO loss, SDE sampler and denoising-reduction procedure remain unchanged. The PDFs do not establish whether implementation changed.

E1.justification: Both versions cover GenEval, generated text-rendering prompts, human preference alignment, DrawBench and T2I-CompBench++, including unseen object classes and unseen counts. The added comparisons and qualitative examples remain within this coverage.

E2.justification: v4 Appendix C.1 adds direct comparisons with online and offline SFT and Flow-DPO on human preference alignment and GenEval (Figures 6–7). Figure 6 also evaluates offline Flow-RWR. These optimizer comparisons are absent from v1; the comparator sets in the retained benchmark tables are unchanged.

E3.justification: The reported KL coefficient changes from 0.004 to 0.04 for GenEval/text rendering and from 0.001 to 0.01 for PickScore. Section 5.1 also revises reward definitions, including the OCR accuracy metric. New comparator experiments specify matched group sizes, fixed offline collectors and online collector updates every 40 steps. These are substantive reported protocol changes; rerunning the retained experiments is not established.

E4.justification: v4 adds DPO beta-sensitivity tests, expanded KL case studies, fixed-prompt image evolution during training, and comparisons of 40-step ODE sampling with 40/10/5-step SDE sampling. The original denoising and KL curves remain as Figures 8–9. v1's account of unsuccessful multi-reward-ensemble experiments is removed.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-training-run counts, evaluation seed counts, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. The added plots continue reporting individual curves without uncertainty estimates; qualitative discussion of different sampling seeds already appears in v1.

E6.justification: New Figures 6–7 report alignment-method learning curves and training-collapse findings, while Figures 10–16 add qualitative outcomes. Table 2 fills previously missing DrawBench PickScore entries with 23.56 without KL and 23.53 with KL for preference-trained models. Existing benchmark numerical entries are otherwise retained despite revised specifications, so they do not establish a same-setting performance improvement. The multi-reward-ensemble failure finding is removed.

T1.justification: Appendix A repairs the existing derivation: v1 Equation 20 incorrectly obtains a negative score term from the forward Fokker–Planck equation; v4 Equation 16 uses the positive term and Equations 18–21 explicitly derive time reversal. The resulting reverse SDE, score–velocity relationship and discretized sampler remain unchanged.

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction retain the claimed first integration of online RL into flow matching, the two main strategies, the 63%–95% GenEval and 59%–92% text-rendering results, and minimal reward hacking. The added conclusion restates these contributions; softer quality-preservation wording does not materially redefine the already qualified claims.

C2.justification: v4 explicitly acknowledges occasional prompt-dependent reward hacking despite KL. It changes the stated deterministic-sampling obstacle from unavailable probabilities to costly divergence estimation, and Appendix D explains how relative rewards remain useful with degraded training samples. The unsuccessful multi-reward discussion is removed, while the central KL and generalization interpretations remain.

D1.justification: v4 documents comparator sample selection, reward weighting, preference-pair construction and collector refresh rules. It identifies GPT4o as the prompt generator, revises KL hyperparameters, clarifies Table 2's evaluation prompt sources and adds a project visualization link. Existing code and model access information is largely retained or relocated.

R1.justification: v4 adds references to Score as Action, Anderson's reverse-time diffusion work, and dedicated DALL-E3 and T2I-CompBench++ papers, while removing the Williams/REINFORCE reference. The principal related-work categories and positioning relative to existing flow and diffusion alignment research remain.

P1.justification: Existing introduction, related-work, method and experimental passages are extensively condensed and rewritten. Numbered method subsections become paragraph headings, metric descriptions move to Appendix B.1, and v4 adds a conclusion, acknowledgements and an organized appendix contents page. This substantially revises the narrative structure beyond adding experiments.

P2.justification: v4 adds comparison plots and extensive qualitative displays in Figures 6–7 and 10–16. Earlier Figures 6–7 become Figures 8–9 and are consolidated on one page; other figures are resized or relocated. Table highlighting and captions also change, including clearer evaluation-source labeling in Table 2.

improvement.justification: v4 addresses two important deficiencies: missing direct comparisons against alternative alignment optimizers and a faulty step in the central SDE derivation. Appendix C.1 strengthens empirical support, while Appendix A repairs the proof; additional diagnostics and explicit residual reward-hacking limitations improve assessment. The unexplained relationship between revised reward/KL specifications and retained scores, plus removal of the failed ensemble discussion, leaves transparency limitations, but the gains in support and mathematical correctness are substantial.
